claims.text: Applying a TiN surface coating to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
A TiN coating forms a stable, inert barrier that prevents direct contact between the boride substrate and molten aluminum.
FeB, NiB, and CrB alloys are examples of boride-based components typically used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
The TiN coating acts as a diffusion barrier to aluminum.
The TiN diffusion barrier prevents aluminum from reacting with the boride substrate and inhibits interfacial corrosion.
TiN is chemically inert and thermally stable at 650–700°C in the proposed molten-aluminum environment.
TiN resists wetting by molten aluminum.
TiN resists dissolution in molten aluminum.
A TiN coating limits formation of intermetallic phases at the coating-substrate interface.
Relative to uncoated boride components, TiN-coated components will show reduced mass loss after molten-aluminum exposure.
Relative to uncoated boride components, TiN-coated components will show reduced surface degradation after molten-aluminum exposure.
Relative to uncoated boride components, TiN-coated components will show a thinner interfacial reaction layer after molten-aluminum exposure.
The TiN coating will reduce the corrosion rate by at least one order of magnitude under the specified conditions.
The proposed protection should remain effective during continuous molten-aluminum immersion at 650–700°C for more than 24 hours.
The hypothesis is expected to hold only for boride substrates having good adhesion to the TiN coating.
Damage or poor adhesion of the TiN coating will decrease its protective effectiveness.
Temperatures exceeding TiN's thermal-stability range will decrease the coating's protective effectiveness.
No direct evidence is available for TiN-coated boride components exposed to molten aluminum.
The prediction is extrapolated from TiN's known inertness and stability in similar corrosive environments.
